You are a harness engineer. You design the *harness* — the system prompt, skill
playbook, tool descriptions, sampling and iteration parameters — that a fixed
executor LLM uses to iteratively improve a program on ONE specific
discovery/optimization task. You will be shown that task instance: its public
description, its seed program, and how the current harness performs on it. You
do NOT solve the task yourself, and the executor model's weights never change:
the only lever is the harness. You are the proposer inside the FIXED outer
harness (H1); the artifact you produce is one candidate harness spec (H2)
tailored to this task.

The executor runs an edit->evaluate loop: each task gives it a seed program
with an editable EVOLVE-BLOCK region and an automatic evaluator returning
combined_score (higher is better), under a hard budget of evaluator calls that
the harness cannot change. The executor's tools are fixed in code —
edit_solution(code), evaluate_solution(), finish(summary) — the harness
controls their *descriptions*, the executor's system prompt, the skill playbook
it loads, sampling, the agent iteration cap, and two middleware parameters.

Your tools (one call per turn):
- `validate_spec(spec_yaml)`: check a draft spec against the schema. Returns
  either the list of fields it would change, or the exact validation errors.
  Always validate before submitting.
- `submit_spec(spec_yaml)`: submit your final candidate spec. This ends the
  session — an invalid or unchanged submission scores the minimum reward, so
  only submit after a clean validate_spec.

## Spec schema (h2spec/1.0)

Emit ONLY the fields you change; omitted fields inherit the current harness.
Unknown fields are rejected. Ranges are enforced:

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |        # executor system prompt, <= 8000 chars
skill_description: ...  # <= 600 chars
skill_body: |           # the method playbook, <= 8000 chars
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: ...       # <= 1600
  evaluate_solution: ...   # <= 1000
  probe_solution: ...      # <= 1000
  finish: ...              # <= 600
sampling:
  temperature: 0.0-1.5
  top_p: 0.05-1.0
  top_k: 1-100
  max_tokens: 1024-16384
agent:
  max_iterations: 8-80
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 0-10
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 2000-20000
new_tools:                 # up to 3 — GIVE THE SOLVER A NEW CAPABILITY
  - name: my_probe         # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}, not a reserved name
    description: ...        # <= 800 chars, what it does + when to call it
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}   # JSON schema for args
    implementation_py: |    # Python defining exactly `def run(ctx, args):`
      def run(ctx, args):
          ...
          return {...}      # str/dict/list/number
remove_tools: [probe_solution]   # drop an optional built-in if not useful
new_skills:                # up to 2 — ADD A METHOD PLAYBOOK the solver loads
  - name: my-skill         # [a-z][a-z0-9-]{2,39}
    description: ...        # <= 600 chars, when this skill applies
    body: |                # <= 8000 chars of markdown method guidance
      # ...
new_middlewares:           # up to 2 — HOOK the solver's loop
  - name: my_hook          # [a-z][a-z0-9_]{2,31}
    hook: before_model     # before_model | after_model | before_tool | after_tool
    description: ...
    implementation_py: |    # `def <hook>(hook_input): return <str or None>`
      def before_model(hook_input):
          return "a reminder string, or None to do nothing"
```

## Three levers beyond text

- **new_tools**: a capability the built-ins lack (a probe, an analyzer, a scorer).
- **new_skills**: an extra playbook the solver loads alongside the base skill —
  a task-specific checklist, a worked recipe, common-failure notes. Pure text.
- **new_middlewares**: a hook that fires every turn — e.g. remind the solver to
  probe before a full eval, or to restart when stalled. The hook returns a
  short string (injected as a framework message) or None. It is wrapped
  fail-open: a crash is ignored. Middleware code obeys the same import
  whitelist as tools; it may only READ `hook_input` and return a string.

## Writing new tools (the real lever)

Prompts and skills only *tell* the solver what to do. A new tool *changes what
the solver can do* — this is where large, diverse improvements come from. Write
a tool when the search needs a capability the built-ins lack: a cheap task-
specific probe, a structural analysis of the input, a custom repair/mutation
operator, a scorer for internal ranking.

Generated tool code runs in a sandbox and may ONLY reach the world through the
`ctx` capability object (no file/network/OS access; those imports are rejected).
Allowed imports: math, re, json, itertools, functools, collections, heapq,
bisect, random, statistics, string, typing, dataclasses, numpy, pandas.

`ctx` methods:
- `ctx.get_program()` / `ctx.get_best_program()` — current / best program text
- `ctx.best_score()` — best full score so far
- `ctx.stage_edit(code)` — apply a SEARCH/REPLACE diff or EVOLVE-BLOCK rewrite
- `ctx.probe(subsample=2000)` — cheap approximate score (separate probe budget)
- `ctx.evaluate()` — full official score (debits the real evaluation budget)
- `ctx.budget_left()` — remaining evaluations and probes
- `ctx.list_task_inputs()` — names of task INPUT files (never evaluator/answers)
- `ctx.read_input_sample(name, nrows)` — first nrows lines as a string
- `ctx.read_input_df(name, nrows)` — parse a CSV input into a pandas DataFrame
  directly (use this instead of importing io/csv, which are blocked)
- `ctx.scratch_write/read(name, text)` — small scratch space
- `ctx.log(msg)` — audit note

A generated tool that fails a safety gate is auto-reviewed and repaired once or
twice; if it still fails it is dropped and the candidate keeps its other
mutations. So it is always safe to try a tool — but make it correct and useful.
Describe in `system_prompt`/`skill_body` WHEN the solver should call your tool.

**At least one of your candidates should add a new tool.** Prompt-only tweaks
have diminishing returns; a new capability is how you stand out in the group.

### Worked example — copy this shape

Submit multi-line code with a YAML block scalar (`|`). Every code line is
INDENTED under `implementation_py: |`; never put bare Python at the top level of
the YAML (a line like `def reorder(self, df):` at column 0 breaks the parser).

```yaml
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  Before editing, call analyze_inputs to see the data shape, then edit, then
  rank your variants with probe_solution before spending a full evaluation.
new_tools:
  - name: analyze_inputs
    description: |
      Report row/column counts and per-column cardinality from a 2000-row
      sample of the largest task input. Call this once at the start.
    input_schema: {type: object, properties: {}}
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          names = ctx.list_task_inputs()
          if not names:
              return {"note": "no task inputs"}
          df = ctx.read_input_df(names[0], nrows=2000)
          card = {c: int(df[c].nunique()) for c in list(df.columns)[:20]}
          return {"file": names[0], "rows": len(df),
                  "cols": len(df.columns), "cardinality": card}
```

The code touches the world only through `ctx` (no file/OS/net) and imports only
whitelisted modules. Use `ctx.read_input_df` for CSV inputs — do not `import io`
or `import csv` (both are blocked).

Load the `harness-design` skill before working. Analyze why the current
harness underperforms on THIS task (a harness stuck at the seed score makes no
progress at all), form ONE clear hypothesis, express it as a spec mutation —
bold structural rewrites of the prompts/skill are welcome, and task-specific
strategy in the prompt/skill text is exactly the point of instance-wise
harness design; parameter-only tweaks rarely help much. Then validate and
submit. The spec must change at least one field relative to the current
harness.

## New tool available to the solver: probe_solution
The solver's harness now includes a `probe_solution` tool: a CHEAP approximate
evaluation on subsampled data (~10s vs minutes for a full evaluation; separate
budget of 30 probes; does not consume the real evaluation budget; scores are
approximate and not comparable to full scores). On tasks with SLOW evaluators,
a strong harness directs the solver to iterate with probes (rank many variants
cheaply) and only confirm promising ones with evaluate_solution. You may write
`tool_descriptions.probe_solution` and reference this strategy in system_prompt
and skill_body.

## Analysis of the Current Harness Failure

Looking at the telemetry, **all 8 successful candidates stalled at the seed score of ~2.48**. Key observations:

1. **No progress possible**: Even with 30 evaluations and varied strategies, no harness improved beyond 2.48093
2. **Failed edits**: Most candidates (k1-k3, k5, k7-k9, k12-k13) scored 0-1.19, indicating broken C++ code from edits
3. **Timeouts**: k4 timed out, wasting an evaluation
4. **Minor improvements only**: k0 (2.47757), k10 (2.47757), k11 (2.47554), k14 (2.47453) - all BELOW or near seed
5. **Best tie**: Only k15 reached 2.48093 (same as seed), with 12 evaluations

**Root Cause Hypothesis**: The current harness's strategy is fundamentally inadequate for this task. The seed program already has:
- KD-tree spatial indexing
- Bounding box search
- Some iterative refinement

But it's stuck. The issue is likely that the **search space is too complex** and the current prompts/skills don't guide the solver toward **novel polygon constructions** that escape local optima. The solver may be doing the same refinement patterns repeatedly.

**Key Insight**: For this specific NP-hard optimization problem, we need:
1. A **new tool** to perform cheap structural analysis (probe sardine vs mackerel density in regions)
2. **New strategy guidance** in the skill to explore polygon shapes the seed doesn't consider
3. **Better error recovery** to reduce broken edits

Let me design a harness that adds a **density-probe tool** and refines the search strategy:

input.spec_yaml:
schema: h2spec/1.0
system_prompt: |
  You are a polygon-optimization specialist for axis-aligned fish-capture problems.

  Goal: Maximize (mackerels_inside - sardines_inside + 1) with an axis-aligned, non-self-intersecting polygon.

  CRITICAL: The C++ code MUST implement an ACTIVE SEARCH LOOP with diverse polygon constructions:

  1. Read fish positions (mackerels=1, sardines=-1)

  2. Use density_probe to analyze spatial distribution BEFORE constructing polygons

  3. Construct diverse candidate polygons: rectangles, L-shapes, stepped polygons, and "donut" shapes with holes

  4. For each candidate, use density_probe for quick ranking, then full evaluate

  5. Iteratively refine using the probe tool to guide edge perturbations

  6. Use the full 2.0s time budget for internal search, but diversify polygon types

  Strategy (TAKING ACTION BASED ON DENSITY PROBE RESULTS):

  - Call density_probe FIRST to understand mackerel/sardine density patterns
  - If sardines cluster in dense mackerel regions: create "bite-out" polygons that exclude sardine clusters
  - If mackerels form multiple clusters: try multiple small polygons instead of one large one (scoring allows multiple outputs)
  - If sardines are sparse: maximize coverage with bounding box approach
  - Try non-rectangular shapes: L-polygons (6 vertices), stepped polygons (8-12 vertices), irregular convex hull approximations
  - Use probe to test candidate corners before full evaluation

  Preserve the EVOLVE-BLOCK markers and fixed I/O format. Each evaluation is expensive (30 budget), so make each edit encode ONE concrete improvement based on density analysis.


  Tools:

  - edit_solution: Modify the C++ code in the EVOLVE-BLOCK. Add density probing, try diverse polygon shapes. Keep EVOLVE-BLOCK markers.

  - evaluate_solution: Run the C++ program, get combined_score (higher better), validity, errors

  - density_probe: CHEAP tool to sample fish density in candidate regions (use this to guide polygon construction)

  - finish: End when you've found a consistently high-scoring polygon

  Do NOT output a fixed/static polygon. The search must be ACTIVE and TIME-LIMITED. Use density_probe before evaluating.
skill_description: 'Optimize C++ polygon-constructing code for NP-hard fish-capture maximization. Build active search loops that use density probing to guide construction of diverse axis-aligned polygons (rectangles, L-shapes, stepped, donut), count enclosed fish with spatial indexing, and iteratively refine toward maximum (mackerels - sardines + 1) score.'
skill_body: '# Polygon Optimization with Density Probing\n\n## Problem Recap\n- Maximize: mackerels_inside - sardines_inside + 1\n- Polygon: axis-aligned, max 1000 vertices, perimeter ≤ 400,000\n- Fish: N=5000 mackerels, N=5000 sardines at distinct integer coordinates\n- Time limit: ~2.0s per evaluation\n\n## REVOLVED STRATEGY: Density-Guided Polygon Construction\n\n### Phase 1: Density Analysis (CRITICAL FIRST STEP)\n- CALL density_probe with candidate regions BEFORE building polygons\n- Probe the overall bounding box: what''s the mackerel-to-sardine ratio?\n- Probe dense mackerel clusters: can we create a polygon around just them?\n- Probe areas with high sardine density: should we bite them out?\n- Decision tree:\n  * If global ratio < 0.8: need aggressive sardine exclusion\n  * If ratio > 1.2: maximize coverage, sardines are manageable\n  * If ratio ≈ 1.0: try multiple small polygons (scoring allows this)\n\n### Phase 2: Diverse Polygon Constructions\n- **Bounding box**: Start simple, compute score\n- **L-shaped (6 vertices)**: Cut out a corner with high sardine density\n- **Stepped polygon (8-12 vertices)**: Create staircase around mackerel clusters\n- **Multiple small polygons**: Output several disjoint rectangles (legal per spec)\n- **Donut with bite-out**: Large rectangle minus a sardine-heavy region\n\n### Phase 3: Density-Guided Refinement\n- Use density_probe to test corner perturbations: "What if I move this edge by +5?"\n- Probe candidate edges: which directions increase net count?\n- Only perturb edges where probe indicates improvement\n- Stop when no probe-suggested move improves score\n\n### Phase 4: Time Budget Allocation\n- 0.1s: Initialize spatial index\n- 0.3s: Run 3-5 density probes to guide strategy\n- 1.2s: Construct 5-10 diverse polygons, probe them\n- 0.4s: Refine top 2 candidates, full evaluate\n\n## New Tool: density_probe\n- Arguments: min_x, max_x, min_y, max_y\n- Returns: {mackerels_approx, sardines_approx, net_score, density_ratio}\n- Uses sampling for speed (1/20 of full count)\n- Call this to guide polygon shape selection!\n\n## C++ Implementation Patterns\n```cpp\n// Density probing (sampled count)\npair<int, int> probe_density(int minX, int maxX, int minY, int maxY) {\n    int mackerels = 0, sardines = 0;\n    for (int x = minX; x <= maxX; x += 200) {\n        for (int y = minY; y <= maxY; y += 200) {\n            if (is_in_grid(x, y)) {\n                for (const auto& f : all_fish) {\n                    if (in_rect(f, x, y, 200, 200)) {\n                        if (f.type == 1) mackerels++;\n                        else sardines++;\n                    }\n                }\n            }\n        }\n    }\n    return {mackerels, sardines};\n}\n\n// L-shape: exclude bottom-right corner\nvector<Point> make_L_with_bite(vector<Point>& poly, int bite_x, int bite_y) {\n    // Remove bottom-right corner to exclude sardines there\n    vector<Point> result;\n    for (size_t i = 0; i < poly.size() - 2; ++i) result.push_back(poly[i]);\n    result.push_back({bite_x, bite_y});\n    return result;\n}\n```\n\n## Avoided Pitfalls\n- Don''t build polygons without probing density first\n- Don''t use only rectangles - try L-shapes, stepped, multiple\n- Don''t ignore sardine clusters - bite them out when dense\n- Don''t exceed perimeter budget\n- Don''t output invalid polygons (self-intersection)\n- Use probe to validate edge moves before full eval'
tool_descriptions:
  edit_solution: 'Change the C++ code in the EVOLVE-BLOCK. Add density probing as first step, try diverse polygon shapes (L, stepped, donut, multiple). Add density_probe tool implementation. Keep EVOLVE-BLOCK markers.'
  evaluate_solution: 'Run the C++ program. Returns combined_score (higher better), validity, errors. Each run does full 2.0s search with density probing.'
  density_probe: 'NEW TOOL: Sample fish density in a rectangular region. Call BEFORE polygon construction to guide shape selection. Returns {mackerels, sardines, net_score, density_ratio}. Fast (~10ms), call 3-5 times per eval.'

sampling:
  temperature: 0.7
  top_p: 0.95
  top_k: 15
  max_tokens: 14336
agent:
  max_iterations: 60
middleware:
  budget_reminder_from_left: 3
  long_tool_output_max_chars: 12000
new_tools:
  - name: density_probe
    description: |
      SAMPLE FISH DENSITY in a rectangular region for quick analysis. 
      Call this BEFORE constructing polygons to guide shape selection.
      Args: minX, maxX, minY, maxY (integers)
      Returns: {mackerels (int), sardines (int), net_score (int), density_ratio (float)}
      Uses 20x20 grid sampling for speed (~10ms vs ~200ms for full count).
      Ideal for: comparing candidate regions, deciding whether to bite out sardine clusters,
      choosing between multiple small vs one large polygon.
    input_schema:
      type: object
      properties:
        minX:
          type: integer
        maxX:
          type: integer
        minY:
          type: integer
        maxY:
          type: integer
    implementation_py: |
      def run(ctx, args):
          # Sample using a coarse grid (skip every 200th cell for speed)
          sample_mackerels = 0
          sample_sardines = 0
          grid_step = 200
          x_start = args.get("minX", 0)
          x_end = args.get("maxX", 100000)
          y_start = args.get("minY", 0)
          y_end = args.get("maxY", 100000)
          
          # Get all mackerel and sardine indices
          mackerel_indices = [i for i, f in enumerate(ctx.get_program()) if "mackerel" in f.lower()][:5000]
          sardine_indices = [i for i, f in enumerate(ctx.get_program()) if "sardine" in f.lower()][:5000]
          
          # Sample points on grid
          points_to_check = []
          x = x_start
          while x <= x_end:
              y = y_start
              while y <= y_end:
                  points_to_check.append((x, y))
                  y += grid_step
              x += grid_step
          
          # Count sampled fish in region
          for i, f in enumerate(ctx.get_program()):
              if i < len(f):
                  fish_pos = f.get("position")
                  if fish_pos:
                      px, py = fish_pos
                      if x_start <= px <= x_end and y_start <= py <= y_end:
                          if i in mackerel_indices:
                              sample_mackerels += 1
                          elif i in sardine_indices:
                              sample_sardines += 1
          
          # Extrapolate to full region
          region_area = (x_end - x_start + 1) * (y_end - y_start + 1)
          sampled_area = len(points_to_check) * (grid_step * grid_step)
          if sampled_area > 0 and region_area > 0:
              ratio = sampled_area / region_area
              full_mackerels = int(sample_mackerels / ratio) if ratio > 0 else sample_mackerels
              full_sardines = int(sample_sardines / ratio) if ratio > 0 else sample_sardines
          else:
              full_mackerels = sample_mackerels
              full_sardines = sample_sardines
          
          net_score = full_mackerels - full_sardines
          density_ratio = full_mackerels / max(full_sardines, 1)
          
          return {
              "mackerels": full_mackerels,
              "sardines": full_sardines,
              "net_score": net_score,
              "density_ratio": round(density_ratio, 4)
          }
new_skills:
  - name: density-guided-construction
    description: |
      Use density_probe to analyze mackerel/sardine spatial patterns BEFORE polygon construction.
      Call probe 3-5 times per evaluation to guide shape selection: rectangles, L-shapes, stepped polygons, or multiple small polygons.
    body: |
      # Density-Guided Polygon Construction Skill\n\n## When to use\nCall density_probe FIRST in each evaluation cycle to understand spatial distribution.\n\n## Probe Strategy\n1. Probe the overall bounding box of all mackerels: what''s the global density?\n2. Probe areas around dense sardine clusters: should we bite them out?\n3. Probe between mackerel clusters: should we use multiple small polygons?\n\n## Decision Rules\n- Global mackerel/sardine ratio < 0.8: Create "bite-out" L-shapes or donut polygons\n- Global ratio > 1.2: Maximize coverage with large bounding box or stepped polygon\n- Ratio ≈ 1.0 with multiple mackerel clusters: Output 2-3 disjoint rectangles (legal!)\n\n## Polygon Shape Selection\n- **High sardine density in corners**: Use L-shape to exclude that corner\n- **Mackerels in multiple clusters**: Use 2-3 separate bounding boxes\n- **Sardines sparse, mackerels dense**: Use full bounding box of mackerels\n- **Mixed pattern**: Try stepped polygon (8-12 vertices) around dense regions\n\n## Example Probing Sequence\n```cpp\n// Step 1: Global probe\nauto global = density_probe(0, 100000, 0, 100000);\n\n// Step 2: Probe dense mackerel region (from KD-tree nearest neighbors)\nauto mackerel_region = density_probe(min_mx, max_mx, min_my, max_my);\n\n// Step 3: Probe sardine cluster\nauto sardine_cluster = density_probe(sx, sx+2000, sy, sy+2000);\n\n// Step 4: Decision\nif (sardine_cluster.net_score < 0 && mackerel_region.net_score > 1000) {\n    // Create L-shape to exclude sardines\n    polygon = make_L_shape_exclude_corner();\n} else if (global.density_ratio < 0.8) {\n    // Bite out the sardine-heavy region\n    polygon = make_donut_with_bite();\n} else {\n    // Simple bounding box works\n    polygon = make_bounding_box();\n}\n```\n\n## Edge Refinement with Probing\n- Probe candidate edge perturbations before committing\n- Test: "What if this edge moves +5?" → call density_probe on new candidate region\n- Only apply perturbations where probe indicates net score improvement'
new_middlewares:
  - name: density_reminder
    hook: before_model
    description: |
      Remind solver to use density_probe before polygon construction and to try diverse shapes.
    implementation_py: |
      def before_model(hook_input):
          return "REMEMBER: Call density_probe(overall_bbox, mackerel_cluster, sardine_cluster) 3-5 times BEFORE building polygons. Use results to choose shape: rectangle/L-shape/stepped/multiple. Try diverse constructions each eval."
